title: Multi-Agent Orchestrator workflow
description: GENERATED — do not edit. Run `python3 build_schema.py` after changing app/keys.json or app/vocabulary.json. This exists so your editor can tell you which keys are legal, which are required and what values they take, before you deploy rather than after.

$schema.description: Points your editor at this file.

$comment.description: Orientation for whoever opens the file. Not read by anything.

agents.description:
One entry per agent, keyed by agent id.

One entry per agent, keyed by agent id, which must match ^[a-zA-Z][a-zA-Z0-9_]*$ (no hyphens — the id becomes part of an AgentCore Runtime name). For `main` and `dedicated` the id is also the folder name under app/subagents/. FOUR KEYS ARE ON EVERY AGENT regardless of placement — name, kind, runtime, produces — and everything after them depends on `runtime`: a local agent has the model group, a remote one has the remote group, and neither has the other's. That is deliberate rather than untidy. A remote agent's `maxTokens` would read as governing its cost while doing nothing, because the model call happens on the far side of a trust boundary.

name.description:
Display name, shown on the diagram, in the timeline and on a review gate.

Read by: registry.py -> agent.name; bff/workflow.py; the UI node title

kind.description:
Whether the step completes inline or is long-running. Presentation only today: the UI shows a chip when it is not "sync".

Read by: registry.py -> agent.kind; bff/workflow.py ships it; index.html renders the chip

Default: "sync"

runtime.description:
Where the step runs. "main" = in-process; "dedicated" = its own AgentCore Runtime; "a2a" = an agent you do NOT operate, reached over the Agent2Agent protocol. Defaults to "main".

Read by: registry.py, subagent_runtimes.tf / orchestrator-stack.ts; the UI chip

Allowed values (runtimes in app/vocabulary.json): 'main', 'dedicated', 'a2a'

Default: "main"

produces.description:
The name of this agent's deliverable, e.g. "claim-decision". Names the asset type, is injected into the task prompt, and is what the framework stamps as `assetType` on the asset.

Read by: nodes.py task prompt; a2a_agent.py _as_asset (the envelope on a remote reply)

model.description:
Bedrock model id for THIS agent. Omit to use orchestrator.defaultModel — no shipped agent sets it; the mechanism is here for when one step needs a bigger model.

Read by: registry.py -> agent.model -> ctx.llm

temperature.description:
Sampling temperature. Defaults to 0, which is what you want for an agent that emits a structured asset. Some models (Claude Sonnet 5, for one) refuse a temperature; the call then goes without it, and the telemetry says so.

Read by: registry.py -> agent.temperature

Default: 0

topP.description:
Nucleus sampling: only the most likely tokens whose probabilities add up to this (0-1) are considered. Unset uses the model's own default. Several Claude models accept either temperature or topP, not both: with topP set, the call leaves the temperature out if the model says so.

Read by: registry.py -> agent.top_p -> ctx.llm

stopSequences.description:
Text that ends the model's reply as soon as it appears (up to 4). Rarely wanted for an agent that returns a JSON asset: a sequence that occurs inside the JSON cuts it off.

Read by: registry.py -> agent.stop_sequences -> ctx.llm

framework.description:
How this agent's code reasons: "plain" (one model call), "strands" (a Strands agent) or "langgraph" (a LangGraph graph). Every one calls the model through the framework, so guardrails, memory, telemetry and evaluations work the same. Read when the Builder or `scaffold.py apply` writes the agent's code; an agent whose code you wrote yourself keeps it.

Read by: scaffold.py apply -> app/subagents/<id>/agent.py

Allowed values (agentFrameworks in app/vocabulary.json): 'plain', 'strands', 'langgraph'

Default: "plain"

output.description:
What this agent produces. "text" is a JSON asset from its model. "image" makes it an image agent: its model writes an image brief (prompt, negative prompt, caption) from the request and the upstream outputs, and an image model renders it; the asset carries the brief and the stored images, which a reviewer sees at the gate. Images are kept in the deployment's own assets bucket and deleted with it.

Read by: scaffold.py apply -> agent.py (image template); registry.py -> agent.output

Default: "text"

image.description:
How an image agent (`output: "image"`) renders. Each image model is served in a few regions only (`imageModels.regionsByModel` in vocabulary.json): the render runs in this deployment's region when it can, else in one in the same geography, else only with `allowCrossRegion: true`. Bedrock's text guardrails and evaluations do not inspect images; the model's own safety filter does, and a filtered image is reported, not returned.

Read by: registry.py -> agent.image -> ctx.image

model.description: The image model, one of `imageModels` in vocabulary.json. Default: Stable Diffusion 3.5 Large.

aspectRatio.description: One of `imageAspectRatios` in vocabulary.json, e.g. "16:9". Default "1:1".

seed.description: Fix it (0-4294967294) to get the same image for the same brief. Unset: a new one each time.

negativePrompt.description: What the image must never show, added to every brief's own negative prompt.

allowCrossRegion.description: Allow the image brief to leave this deployment's geography when the model is not served in it (vocabulary.json imageModels.regionsByModel). Default false: such a deploy is refused rather than sending the brief abroad silently. A US deployment renders in us-west-2 without it.

vision.description:
Let this agent's model READ images produced earlier in the same run: each of its model calls gets them as image content next to the text. The model must accept image input (Claude, Amazon Nova Pro/Lite, Llama 3.2 Vision, ...); one that does not fails the call with the model's reason. Images never leave the run: only keys under this run's own folder in the assets bucket are read. Bedrock's text guardrails and evaluations do not inspect images.

Read by: registry.py -> agent.vision -> ctx.llm -> images.load_for, llm.run_llm

from.description: Agents that run before this one whose images this agent's model sees — an image agent, or any agent whose output lists `images` with an `imageKey`.

maxImages.description: At most this many images per model call, in the order `from` names the agents (1-20). Default 4.

attachments.description:
Let this agent's model READ the files a run is started with: documents (PDF, Word, Excel, CSV, HTML, text, Markdown, JSON...) and images uploaded on Start run, or named there as s3:// paths in a bucket orchestrator.attachments.s3 allows. Each of its model calls gets them as content next to the text (at most 5 files; documents up to 4.5 MB, images 3.75 MB). The model must accept them (Claude, Amazon Nova, ...). The files are copied into the run's own folder when it starts, so a re-run reads the same ones. Bedrock's text guardrails do not inspect them.

Read by: registry.py -> agent.attachments -> ctx.llm -> attachments.load_for, llm.run_llm; bff/runfiles.py; images.tf / orchestrator-stack.ts assets bucket

Default: false

maxTokens.description:
Output token budget. Required, because too low does not surface as "budget exceeded" — it surfaces as an unparseable asset, so the number belongs in front of you rather than defaulted in code.

Read by: registry.py -> agent.max_tokens

Default: 4000

source.description:
Reach the A2A server this framework deploys for you, instead of an external URL. The deploy injects its endpoint, so there is nothing to commit. Exclusive with agentCard.

Read by: registry.py A2A_SOURCES; a2a.tf / orchestrator-stack.ts inject A2A_ENDPOINTS

Allowed values (a2aSources in app/vocabulary.json): 'a2a_lambda'

agentCard.description:
An external agent's base URL or Agent Card URL. Must be https:// — the request may carry a bearer token. Exclusive with source.

Read by: a2a_agent.py; validated in all three planes

skill.description:
Which of the shipped stand-in's skills this agent is. Only meaningful with `source`: an external agent advertises its own skills in its Agent Card.

Read by: a2a.tf / orchestrator-stack.ts, as the path segment of the injected endpoint

Allowed values (a2aLambdaSkills in app/vocabulary.json): 'compliance', 'resilience', 'analysis', 'recommendation'

Default: "compliance"

auth.description:
How this deployment authenticates TO the remote agent. Must be "sigv4" with `source`, because that endpoint is IAM-authed. A bearer token never goes here — it is injected by the IaC, keyed by agent id.

Read by: a2a_agent.py; validated in all three planes

Allowed values (a2aAuthModes in app/vocabulary.json): 'none', 'bearer', 'oauth2', 'sigv4'

Default: "none"

tool.description:
The tool(s) this agent reads: one key in the `tools` block, or a list of them (e.g. ["policyDocs", "claimsDb"]). Each is queried before the agent reasons and its results are handed to the model as evidence. Validated — a name that does not resolve fails at plan/synth, not at run time. Omit and the agent reasons purely over upstream outputs.

Read by: registry.py -> agent.tools (agent.tool = the first) -> _shared/evidence.gather -> ctx.call_tool / ctx.retrieve

corpus.description:
For the agent's type="kb" tool: which corpus to retrieve from. Must be one of that tool's declared `corpora`, and the Cedar permit is narrowed to it. Requires a kb among the agent's `tool`(s).

Read by: registry.py -> agent.corpus -> ctx.retrieve(doc_type=)

access.description:
A short human label for the data source, for the UI chip. ONLY read when the agent has no `tool` — with a tool the chip comes from the tool's type, so setting both means this is never shown.

Read by: bff/workflow.py data_source -> the UI chip

toolMode.description:
Who decides which tools to call. "direct": every tool the agent is bound to is queried with the request before the model reasons (predictable: one call per tool). "model": the model sees each tool's name, description and input schema, and decides which to call and with what arguments, reading each result before the next — up to maxToolCalls. Every call still goes through the Gateway, so the Cedar policy, the corpus scope and a tool's fixed `args` still apply; each call is on the run's timeline and in Observability.

Read by: registry._configure -> ctx.tool_mode -> evidence.gather -> tool_loop

Allowed values (toolModes in app/vocabulary.json): 'direct', 'model'

Default: "direct"

skills.description:
Skills this agent may use: names in the build's `skills`. Each is know-how written as a SKILL.md (when to use it, then the steps), with optional reference files. With toolMode "model" the agent sees each skill's name and description and opens the ones it needs (use_skill); otherwise its skills are added to its instructions in full.

Read by: registry._configure -> ctx.skills -> ctx.llm, tool_loop (app/common/skills.py)

registry.description:
Where this came from in an AWS Agent Registry (the Builder's Add from registry): {"registryId", "recordId", "name", "version", "sync"}. With sync true, the console refreshes it from the registry record's latest approved version when the build is opened and before each deploy; with sync false it stays as imported and the Builder says when a newer version exists. Read only by the console, never deployed.

Read by: bff/registry.py (the Builder); not deployed

version.description: The record version this was taken from.

sync.description: Keep it in sync with the record's latest approved version.

maxToolCalls.description:
With toolMode "model": the most tool calls the model may make before it must work with what it has. Each call costs a Gateway call and a model turn.

Read by: registry._configure -> ctx.max_tool_calls -> tool_loop

Default: 6

longTerm.description:
Long-term memory strategies: "semantic" extracts discrete facts and insights across runs, "summary" keeps a running summary of each run, "userPreference" learns the preferences, choices and style of whoever runs the agent, "episodic" records what happened in a run (situation, intent, outcome) and reflects on it across runs. The framework recalls before run() and stores after. `true` is shorthand for ["semantic"]. userPreference and episodic are provisioned only when an agent names them: each strategy is a model call per stored turn.

Read by: context.py _longterm_strategies; validated by registry.validate_features

Allowed values (memoryStrategies in app/vocabulary.json): 'semantic', 'summary', 'userPreference', 'episodic'

scope.description:
Whose memories these are. "user" (default): each user's own — one user's runs never feed another's. "subject": shared by everyone for the run's subject_id (a customer, a case), per user when a run has none. "agent": shared by everyone who runs this agent. "run": this run only. The framework builds the memory actor from it, so no namespace can reach another scope.

Read by: context.py _memory_actor

Allowed values (memoryScopes in app/vocabulary.json): 'user', 'subject', 'agent', 'run'

Default: "user"

custom.description:
A custom long-term strategy of this agent's own: a built-in one (`base`: semantic, summary or userPreference) whose extraction follows YOUR `instructions` (what to keep, what to ignore) with the `model` you name (default: the workflow's default model). {"base": "semantic", "instructions": "Keep only the customer's product configuration and open issues."}. Recalled like the others.

Read by: orchestrator-stack.ts CustomMemoryStrategy, main.tf custom_memory_strategy, context.py _namespace_for

use.description:
Use a memory defined in `memories` (its strategies, expiry and scope) instead of setting them here. Each one is its own AgentCore Memory, so agents that name the same memory share what it holds, within its scope.

Read by: context.py _memory_def / memory client MEMORIES; main.tf, orchestrator-stack.ts named memories

input.description:
Screen this agent's input before the model sees it. Use on any agent that reads text a human typed.

Read by: context.py guardrail("INPUT")

output.description:
Screen this agent's output. Use on any agent handling untrusted text.

Read by: context.py guardrail("OUTPUT")

guardrailId.description:
Use a DIFFERENT guardrail for this one agent, instead of the deployment's own. For a step whose content policy genuinely differs — a medical or legal stage inside a general pipeline. Omit and the deployment guardrail applies.

Read by: context.py guardrail() -> the GuardrailIdentifier on the Bedrock call

use.description:
Apply a guardrail defined in `guardrails` instead of the deployment's own (the `guardrail` block). Turn on `input` and/or `output` to say where.

Read by: context.py guardrail() via GUARDRAILS; guardrail.tf, orchestrator-stack.ts named guardrails

enabled.description:
Turn on AgentCore Evaluations for this agent and show its Evaluate button.

Read by: evaluations/service.py is_enabled; bff/workflow.py evalAgents

auto.description:
true scores the agent automatically when the run completes; false means on demand only. Each evaluator is a billed model call, so false is the cheaper default.

Read by: evaluations/service.py is_auto

evaluators.description:
Which judges to run: any of the 13 built-in evaluators (Builtin.<Name>; the session- and tool-call-level ones — GoalSuccessRate, ToolSelectionAccuracy, ToolParameterAccuracy — are not scored by this framework yet), and Custom.<name> for one you define in `evaluations.custom`. A custom one is always run, listed or not. A custom one is either this agent's own (`evaluations.custom`) or one defined for the whole build in `evaluators`.

Read by: evaluations/service.py evaluators_for; shape-checked by registry.validate_features

Default: ["Builtin.Faithfulness"]

custom.description:
Your own LLM-as-a-judge evaluators for this agent: [{"name": "policyTone", "instructions": "Score how well the reply keeps to our policy wording...", "model": "..." (the judge; default the workflow's default model), "scale": [{"value": 1, "label": "Good", "definition": "..."}, ...] (default: a five-point scale from 0 to 1)}]. The framework creates each as an AgentCore evaluator, scores the agent's output with it like a built-in, and deletes it on destroy. The instructions may use {context} and {assistant_turn}; when they use neither, both are appended.

Read by: orchestrator-stack.ts CfnEvaluator, evaluations.tf aws_bedrockagentcore_evaluator, CUSTOM_EVALUATORS -> evaluations/service.py

outbound.description:
Identities this agent may get a credential from, to call an external API DIRECTLY: names from `identities` (the framework creates their AgentCore Identity providers), or the names of providers that already exist in the account. Not needed for anything reached through the Gateway. Required when a remote agent's `auth` is "oauth2".

Read by: context.py get_identity_token / get_api_key via IDENTITY_PROVIDERS

enabled.description:
An app-level Cedar check via ctx.policy_check. Secondary — tool calls through the Gateway are already authorized server-side by the attached engine.

Read by: context.py policy_check

agentcore.description: The AgentCore feature switches: memory, guardrails, evaluations, identity, policy. Omit a block to leave that capability off. See the `agentcore` spec.

then.$comment: A remote agent's URL is either a stable value you write down (an external partner's card) or one the deploy generates (the stand-in's Function URL) and therefore cannot be committed. Both set is ambiguous; neither leaves the agent with nowhere to call.

Omit any key and that policy block is not created at all; omit the whole block (or every policy key) and no build-wide guardrail is created, since Bedrock rejects an empty one. Read only by the IaC: the app just gets a GUARDRAIL_ID.

groupsClaim.description:
The JWT claim holding the caller's groups. Defaults to "cognito:groups".

Read by: bff/authz.py

Default: "cognito:groups"

actions.description:
Action -> the group names allowed to take it. Each action name is a route in bff/handler.py; one with no route would read as a restriction and gate nothing. An action you omit is UNRESTRICTED.

Read by: bff/authz.py; bff/workflow.py projects it to the UI

Allowed keys (authorizationActions in app/vocabulary.json): 'start', 'decision', 'rerun', 'cancel', 'evaluate', 'insights', 'delete', 'deploy', 'destroy', 'audit', 'admin'

provider.description:
Who signs people in to this app: "cognito" (the default: the deployment creates the user list), or your own "okta", "auth0" or "entra" (Microsoft Entra ID). Register the app's address at your provider as its sign-in and sign-out redirect. A console build deploys with it; a deployment of your own sets the same in its idp setting (terraform.tfvars / CDK context), which must agree.

Read by: deployer/runner.py -> idp; terraform/identity.tf, orchestrator-stack.ts check it matches

Allowed values (signInProviders in app/vocabulary.json): 'cognito', 'okta', 'auth0', 'entra'

Default: "cognito"

domain.description:
Okta or Auth0: your org's host, e.g. acme.okta.com or acme.us.auth0.com. No https://, no path.

Read by: deployer/runner.py -> oktaDomain / auth0Domain

clientId.description:
Okta, Auth0 or Entra ID: the client ID of the single-page application registered for this app.

Read by: deployer/runner.py -> oktaClientId / auth0ClientId / entraClientId

tenantId.description:
Entra ID: the Directory (tenant) ID, a GUID. Not a domain name, common or organizations: those would let other tenants sign in.

Read by: deployer/runner.py -> entraTenantId

authorizationServer.description:
Okta: the custom authorization server's ID. "default" unless you made another.

Read by: deployer/runner.py -> oktaAuthServer

Default: "default"

authorization.description: Who may act on a run. An action ABSENT from the `actions` map is unrestricted, so this block is an opt-in list of restrictions rather than a full policy. Enforced in the BFF, and projected to the UI so it can disable a control it knows will 403 instead of offering it and failing.

guardrails.description: Named guardrails for this build, beside the deployment's own `guardrail`. Each entry has the keys of the `guardrail` block and becomes its own Bedrock Guardrail; an agent applies one with agentcore.guardrails.use. Optional.

contentFilters.description:
Filter type -> strength, applied to input and output. PROMPT_ATTACK is input-only, so its output strength is forced to NONE.

Read by: guardrail.tf, orchestrator-stack.ts buildGuardrail

Allowed values (guardrailFilterStrengths in app/vocabulary.json): 'NONE', 'LOW', 'MEDIUM', 'HIGH'

deniedWords.description:
Exact custom terms to block.

Read by: guardrail.tf, buildGuardrail

managedWordLists.description:
AWS-managed lists, e.g. PROFANITY.

Read by: guardrail.tf, buildGuardrail

deniedTopics.description:
Topics to refuse. Each needs a `name` and a `definition` — a definition is what Bedrock actually matches on, so one without it silently blocks nothing. `examples` optional.

Read by: guardrail.tf, buildGuardrail

piiEntities.description:
Bedrock PII entity type -> BLOCK or ANONYMIZE.

Read by: guardrail.tf, buildGuardrail

Allowed values (guardrailPiiActions in app/vocabulary.json): 'BLOCK', 'ANONYMIZE'

blockedInputMessage.description:

Read by: guardrail.tf, buildGuardrail

blockedInputMessage.default: This request was blocked by the content guardrail.

files.description:

Read by: app/common/skills.py

registry.description:
